common_name: Gay Butterflies Butterfly Weed (Mixed-Color Butterfly Milkweed Strain)

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost, or start indoors and transplant, into well-drained, average-to-lean soil in full sun; this open-pollinated seed strain of butterfly weed produces a mix of orange, yellow, and red-orange flowered plants from the same sowing.

directions: Sow in well-drained, lean-to-average soil in full sun; like the wild species, Gay Butterflies resents wet feet and rich, heavily amended soil and performs best where it is left largely undisturbed once established. This heirloom seed strain was selected to broaden the color range of straight butterfly weed, producing a mix of orange, gold, yellow, and red-orange umbels on the same deep, drought-tolerant taproot that makes the species so tough in poor, dry sites. It is a larval host for monarch caterpillars and a strong nectar draw for a wide range of butterflies, bees, and other pollinators through a long summer bloom season. Because the taproot resents transplanting once mature, direct-sow where plants are to remain or transplant only small, young seedlings, and expect variable bloom color to appear starting the second year.

common_name: Soulmate Swamp Milkweed (Compact Rose-Pink Native Milkweed Selection)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun; Soulmate is a compact selection of swamp milkweed bred to stay shorter and more floriferous than the wild species without losing its wetland toughness.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun; Soulmate is a compact selection of the native swamp milkweed, bred to stay a shorter, tidier 18 to 24 inches while still producing the dense, rose-pink, vanilla-scented flower clusters that make the species a monarch and pollinator magnet. Its shorter, sturdier habit fits more easily into a mixed perennial border or rain garden than the taller wild species, which can reach four feet or more, while still tolerating the wet soils and occasional standing water it needs to thrive. As a larval host for monarch butterflies and a heavy nectar source for many other butterflies and native bees, it is a strong choice for a pollinator garden with a moist low spot or pond margin. Cut back spent flower stalks after seed pods form to prevent excess self-seeding, or leave pods to split and release silky-tufted seed for wildlife interest.

common_name: Alma Potschke Aster (Hot Pink New England Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Alma Potschke is a New England aster selection prized for its unusually vivid, glowing rose-pink flowers rather than the species' typical purple.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Alma Potschke is a long-popular New England aster cultivar named for the German nurserywoman who discovered it as a sport, valued for its intensely saturated, glowing rose-pink daisy flowers with yellow centers that stand out from the more common purple-flowered forms of the species. It blooms heavily from late summer into fall, providing critical late-season nectar for monarch butterflies staging for migration as well as bees and other pollinators when few other perennials are still flowering. Plants can become tall and somewhat floppy by bloom time; pinching stems back by a third in early summer encourages bushier, more self-supporting growth and delays flowering slightly. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and control its spreading habit.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or start indoors with a moist chilling period, into average, well-drained soil in full sun; early goldenrod tolerates poor, dry soils and is among the first goldenrods to bloom, often starting in mid to late summer.

directions: Plant in average to poor, well-drained soil in full sun; early goldenrod is remarkably tolerant of dry, rocky, or sandy sites and needs no supplemental feeding or watering once established. True to its common name, it is one of the earliest goldenrods to bloom, opening its smooth, arching, plume-like clusters of small golden flowers in mid to late summer well ahead of most other Solidago species, extending the nectar season for bees and butterflies. Its smooth stems and glossy, hairless leaves distinguish it from many rougher-textured goldenrod relatives, and it forms a tidy clump that spreads modestly by rhizome rather than aggressively colonizing. Cut back after flowering if a neater fall appearance is wanted, or leave seed heads standing through winter to feed goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

planting.note: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost; Floristan White is the white-flowered counterpart to the classic Floristan Violet gayfeather, sharing the same tall, uniform flower spikes.

directions: Plant corms in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, avoiding heavy, waterlogged ground that can rot the corms over winter. Floristan White is a long-cultivated selection of native dense blazing star bred for tall, densely packed, pure white bottlebrush spikes that open from the top down, an unusual flowering pattern among spike-forming perennials, and pairs naturally with its violet-flowered Floristan Violet sibling in cut-flower and pollinator plantings. Like the species, it draws heavy traffic from butterflies, bees, and other pollinators through its summer bloom season and provides seed for finches if spikes are left standing into fall. Its reliable, uniform habit and strong stems have made it a mainstay of the commercial cut-flower trade as well as the perennial border; divide congested corm clusters every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.

common_name: Bartered Bride Joe Pye Weed (White-Flowered Spotted Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Bartered Bride is a white-flowered sport of spotted Joe-Pye weed discovered at the Chicago Botanic Garden, otherwise similar in scale and habit to the species.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Bartered Bride is a striking white-flowered selection of spotted Joe-Pye weed, discovered as a naturally occurring color break and named for its unusual pure white, domed flower clusters that stand out against the green foliage rather than the mauve-pink typical of the species. It reaches the same imposing size as wild spotted Joe-Pye weed and draws the same heavy traffic from swallowtails, monarchs, and countless bees during its late-summer bloom, making it a good way to add color contrast to a large pollinator planting, rain garden, or pond edge without losing habitat value. Give it plenty of room and reliably moist soil, since it will decline quickly in dry conditions, and divide clumps in spring every several years if a larger planting is desired. Leave seed heads standing into winter for visual interest and songbird forage.

common_name: Twilite Prairieblues Baptisia (Bicolor Violet-and-Yellow False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Twilite Prairieblues is a hybrid between Baptisia australis and Baptisia sphaerocarpa bred at the Chicago Botanic Garden, combining traits of both native parents.

directions: Plant in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; like its native Baptisia parents, Twilite Prairieblues develops a substantial taproot and strongly resents transplanting once established, so choose a permanent site from the start. This hybrid of blue wild indigo and yellow wild indigo produces striking bicolor flower spikes that open deep violet-purple and age to smoky charcoal-lilac with yellow-tinged keels, combining the vigor and bicolor interest of both native species into a single robust, shrub-like clump. It flowers over a long spring season and is heavily visited by bumblebees and other native bees, while the blue-green foliage and blackening seed pods provide structure through summer and fall. Established plants are extremely drought- and heat-tolerant and need no staking, fertilizing, or division, making them essentially maintenance-free once their deep root system is in place.
